title: Vayigash: few and evil days (Genesis 47:9)
hookLine: asked his age, Jacob tells Pharaoh his years have been hard

cards: Busy. It's the standard answer at the coffee machine, even in a year when a marriage is ending, or a parent is sick, or the work has dried up. A small social lie, and an easy one.
Now an elderly shepherd, just arrived in a foreign country, stands before the king of Egypt. The king makes polite conversation: how old are you? Jacob could say a number and smile.

teach.h: AN OLD MAN BLESSES A KING.
teach.b: Joseph brings his father to meet Pharaoh. Jacob blesses the king, an old man blessing a ruler, which already tells you something. Pharaoh asks, roughly, how many years have you lived?

Jacob answers: a hundred and thirty years of wandering. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "few and evil" have been the days of my life, and they haven't reached the years of my fathers.
In Hebrew, me'at v'ra'im. Few and hard. Think about what he's carrying.
He fled a brother who wanted to kill him. His father-in-law cheated him for twenty years. His beloved Rachel died on the road.
His daughter Dinah was violated. For years he believed his favorite son was dead. That's the honest summary, and he gives it to a king.

teach.h: ADMIRED BY SOME, FAULTED BY OTHERS.
teach.b: Some admire it: no pretending, not even before Pharaoh. Others think he complained to the wrong person at the wrong moment, just after his son was found alive.
A medieval tradition even counts the words of the conversation and says each word of complaint cost him a year.
Jacob lives to a hundred and forty-seven, fewer than his father or grandfather. Either way, the Torah keeps the answer. It lets a patriarch say out loud: my life has been hard.
And then it lets him bless the king anyway, on his way out.

how: Honest lament has a long home in Jewish prayer, from the Psalms and the Book of Lamentations, read on Tisha b'Av, to the custom of speaking openly about the dead and one's loss during the week of shiva.

o: and he wept, Joseph's cry as he reveals himself
and he went down, the family's move into Egypt
and he drew near, the portion that brings Jacob to Egypt

games.q: Jacob before Pharaoh — tap the pairs.
p: asked how many years he had lived

s: Jacob gave Pharaoh a polite, cheerful answer
he said his days had been few and evil, and fewer than his fathers'.
the text says Jacob blessed Pharaoh, coming in and going out.
some admire his honesty; others fault him for complaining, especially just after finding Joseph.

games.q: you're Jacob, newly arrived in Egypt. the king asks how old you are. what do you say?
o: just the number, with a smile.
the number, and the truth that the years were hard.
that your life has been richly blessed.
games.why: Jacob said a hundred and thirty, and that his days had been few and evil. then he blessed Pharaoh and left.

practice: Find one stretch of your own years that was genuinely hard, one you usually sum up as fine, and name it to yourself plainly, the way Jacob did: that year was hard. No drama, no fixing.
Then, if you can, find one thing from it you'd still bless, the way Jacob blessed the king on his way out.

wordCard.voice: Vayigash. The portion that ends with Jacob in Egypt, telling Pharaoh the truth: his years have been few and hard.

orig.note: Hebrew: few and evil, few and hard. Jacob's summary of his life (Genesis 47:9).

carryVoice: Your line: honest about the years. Even a patriarch gets to say it was hard. Day two hundred fifteen, done.
